headline: A trade deal, then Wuhan is locked down
text: On 15 January the US and China signed a 'phase one' trade deal: China will buy $200 billion more of US goods and services over two years. On 23 January China sealed off the city of Wuhan to stop a new coronavirus, and lockdowns spread to other cities.
imageCaption: Signing of the phase-one trade deal, White House, 15 January 2020

headline: Shanghai and profits send Tesla soaring
text: Tesla said on 29 January that 2019 was a turning point: it returned to profit in the second half and generated 1.1 billion dollars of free cash flow. Its Shanghai factory, its first outside the US, started building the Model 3 less than ten months after construction began, and production of the Model Y has started in Fremont. The shares rose more than 50% in January.
source: Tesla Q4 and FY2019 Update, 29 January 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1318605/000156459020002489/tsla-ex991_340.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. (Gigafactory Shanghai, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Aerial view of the Tesla Gigafactory in Shanghai

headline: Soleimani killed, then Iran shoots down a Ukrainian airliner
text: A US drone strike killed General Qasem Soleimani, head of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, at Baghdad airport on 3 January. Iran fired missiles at US bases in Iraq on 8 January; hours later the Revolutionary Guards shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 after take-off from Tehran, killing all 176 aboard, among them 82 Iranians and 63 Canadians, many of them Iranian-Canadian students and academics. After three days of denial, Iran admitted on 11 January that it had downed the plane by mistake, and protesters took to the streets.
imageCaption: US paratroopers deploy to the Middle East, 4 January 2020
imageCredit: Photo by Spc. Hubert Delany, 49th Public Affairs Detachment

headline: The coronavirus reaches the markets: the fastest fall from a record
text: The S&P 500 closed at a record 3,386.15 on 19 February. Then the new coronavirus spread beyond China, and in the week of 24 to 28 February markets had their largest weekly falls since the 2008 crisis, the fastest slide from a record ever seen. The S&P 500 ended February down 8% at 2,954.22.
imageCaption: The new coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 under the electron microscope

headline: Thiam resigns over the spying affair
text: In the final months of 2019 it emerged that Credit Suisse had had former executives, among them the wealth manager Iqbal Khan, followed by private detectives; the chief operating officer Pierre-Olivier Bouée left. On 7 February Tidjane Thiam announced his resignation as chief executive. Thomas Gottstein, head of the Swiss bank, succeeds him on 14 February. At the end of the month markets began to fall as the coronavirus spread.
imageCaption: Tidjane Thiam at the World Economic Forum's Annual Meeting of the New Champions, 2011

headline: The virus reaches Europe and Switzerland
text: The new coronavirus, which the World Health Organization declared an international emergency on 30 January, spread from China to northern Italy in late February, where towns were sealed off. Switzerland confirmed its first case on 25 February, a man in Ticino who had visited Milan, and on 28 February banned events with more than 1,000 people. Stock markets fell in the last week of the month.
imageCaption: Shoppers at a supermarket in Bergamo, Lombardy, 26 February 2020

headline: The virus scare hits oil
text: From 20 February stock markets fell sharply as the coronavirus spread beyond China to South Korea, Italy and Iran; in the last week of February Wall Street fell more than 10 percent. Oil fell with them: US crude closed February at about 45 dollars, from 61 at the end of December. ExxonMobil had already reported in January that its 2019 profit fell 31 percent to 14.3 billion dollars.
imageCaption: An Exxon service station

headline: Pandemic on top of the MAX: Boeing suspends its dividend
text: With air travel collapsing because of Covid-19 and the MAX still grounded, Boeing on 20 March suspended its dividend and extended its halt on buybacks; chief executive Dave Calhoun gives up his pay for the year. On 23 March it said it will stop production in the Seattle area for 14 days.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/12927/000001292720000030/exhibit991.htm (Boeing release of 2020-03-20, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/12927/000001292720000033/exhibit991.htm (Boeing release of 2020-03-23, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Boeing's Everett factory, Washington, from the air

headline: Iger hands over to Chapek; then the pandemic closes the parks
text: On 25 February Bob Iger stepped down as chief executive and was succeeded by Bob Chapek, head of the parks division; Iger stays as executive chairman. In mid-March, as the coronavirus spread, Disney closed Disneyland, Walt Disney World and Disneyland Paris and suspended its cruises; its parks in Asia were already shut. Cinemas closed too.
imageCaption: Bob Chapek, 2019 ;;

headline: Covid crash
text: Global stock markets crashed in March as the coronavirus spread, with the worst day on 16 March. Brent oil averaged $33 a barrel, against $64 in January, and copper $5,183 a tonne. Glencore says its mines have not been materially disrupted and it has $10bn of undrawn credit and cash; on 31 March it postponed its planned $2.6bn shareholder distribution and refinanced $14.6bn of credit lines.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash; https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/glencore--glen/update-on-covid-19/6071958; https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/glencore--glen/2020-distribution-and-revolving-credit-facilities/6205549; World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages (all read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Empty mask shelves in a drugstore, 16 March 2020

headline: Pandemic closes restaurants, stadiums and cinemas: Coca-Cola falls 17%
text: As the coronavirus spread, governments ordered people to stay at home and closed restaurants, bars, cinemas and stadiums, and stock markets crashed. Coca-Cola sells a large part of its drinks through such places. Its shares lost about 17% in March, more than the S&P 500.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/21344/000002134420000011/a2020q1earningsrelease.htm (released 21 April 2020, used for hindsight only, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Coca-Cola scoreboard at a baseball stadium

headline: Pandemic crash: circuit breakers, zero rates and a 34 percent fall
text: As lockdowns spread and Saudi Arabia started an oil price war, trading was halted by circuit breakers on 9, 12 and 16 March; on 16 March the S&P 500 fell 12% and the VIX fear index closed at a record 82.69. The Fed cut rates to zero on 15 March and on 23 March promised unlimited bond buying; that day the S&P 500 fell to 2,237, 34% below the February record, and Congress passed a 2 trillion dollar rescue on 27 March. The S&P 500 ended March down 13% at 2,584.59.
imageCaption: Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell announces an emergency half-point rate cut, Washington, 3 March 2020

headline: Pandemic: dining rooms close, drive-thrus stay open
text: As governments ordered shutdowns, McDonald's said on 16 March that substantially all US restaurants were serving only through drive-thru, delivery and takeaway, and that all restaurants in Italy and Spain, and later France and Britain, were closed. It is working with franchisees on rent deferrals. The shares lost about 15% in March.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390820000024/form8kmainbody.htm (8-K of 16 March 2020, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/63908/000006390820000026/form8kmainbody.htm (8-K of 25 March 2020, read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/mcd.json
imageCaption: A McDonald's drive-thru

headline: The pandemic shuts the car factories
text: As the coronavirus spread across Europe and America, stock markets crashed; on 12 March the DAX fell 12%, one of its worst days ever. Car makers including Daimler halted production in Europe and the United States.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); WCIV, 'Mercedes-Benz stops production at North Charleston van plant over COVID-19', 23 March 2020 (headline via Google News) (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Mercedes-Benz plant in Sindelfingen, Germany

headline: Saudi-Russian price war as the world locks down
text: Russia rejected OPEC's call for deeper cuts on 6 March. Saudi Arabia answered by cutting its prices and announcing it would raise output from 9.7 to 12.3 million barrels a day. On 9 March oil fell about a quarter and stock markets crashed. As lockdowns spread, US crude fell to $20.48 on 18 March and ended the month down 54%.
imageCaption: An oil pumpjack

headline: Back to zero, and unlimited bond buying
text: As the coronavirus spread, the Fed cut its rate by half a point on 3 March and, on Sunday 15 March, to 0 to 0.25 percent, with at least 500 billion dollars of Treasury and 200 billion of mortgage-bond purchases. On 23 March it promised to buy bonds 'in the amounts needed' and, for the first time, to buy corporate bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 0.9 percent in March, a record low.
imageCaption: Jerome Powell chairs a Federal Open Market Committee meeting held by video

headline: Price war and pandemic: Schlumberger halves in a month
text: On 6 March Russia refused OPEC's proposal to cut output; Saudi Arabia answered on 8 March with discounts and more production, and Brent crude fell 30 percent. With the pandemic shutting down economies, US crude closed March at about 20 dollars, from 45 a month earlier.
imageCaption: A semi-submersible drilling rig laid up in a Scottish firth

headline: Pandemic: the world shuts down
text: The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March. Italy locked down on 9 March, the United States barred travellers from Europe, and on 16 March the Swiss government declared an 'extraordinary situation', closing schools, shops, restaurants and borders; on 20 March it announced a 42 billion franc aid package. Stock markets crashed: the Dow lost 7.8 percent on 9 March, 10 percent on 12 March and 12.9 percent on 16 March. The Fed cut rates to zero, and Congress passed a 2.2 trillion dollar relief law on 27 March.
imageCaption: On a balcony during the coronavirus lockdown, Milan, 19 March 2020

headline: Price war and pandemic: oil halves in a month
text: On 6 March Russia refused OPEC's proposal to cut output; on 8 March Saudi Arabia announced discounts of 6 to 8 dollars a barrel and more production, and Brent crude fell 30 percent, the biggest drop since the Gulf War. With countries shutting down against the pandemic, US crude closed March at about 20 dollars, from 45 at the end of February.
imageCaption: Refinery smokestacks on the Texas coast

headline: The pandemic halts BMW's factories
text: The coronavirus crashed stock markets worldwide in March; on 12 March the DAX fell 12%. Car makers stopped their factories; BMW's British plants are shut from 23 March.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW (UK plants shut from 23 March 2020, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Aerial view of the BMW plant at Dingolfing, Germany

headline: Pandemic crash hits bank shares
text: As the coronavirus spread, the Federal Reserve cut its policy rate to near zero on 15 March, saying the outbreak had disrupted economic activity in many countries. Banks face a wave of loan losses and near-zero interest rates for as long as the downturn lasts; Citigroup's shares fell 34% in March.
imageCaption: The empty streets of New York's Financial District, 29 March 2020

headline: The pandemic grounds GE's engine business
text: As Covid-19 spread, air travel collapsed and stock markets had their worst days since 1987. General Electric's biggest profit maker is jet engines and their servicing, paid by the hours airlines fly. Factory workers protested to demand that jet engine plants make ventilators.
imageCaption: A GE90 engine on a Boeing 777-300ER

headline: Switzerland shuts down
text: On 16 March the Federal Council declared an 'extraordinary situation' under the epidemics law because of the coronavirus. Schools, shops other than food stores, restaurants and bars are closed, and from 20 March gatherings of more than five people are banned. Many parents work from home. Disney+ started in Switzerland on 24 March, just in time.
imageCaption: Swiss aircraft grounded during the coronavirus shutdown, March 2020

headline: The pandemic sends shoppers to Amazon
text: With shops closed by the Covid-19 pandemic, Amazon is hiring about 175,000 extra warehouse and delivery workers. On April 30 it reported first-quarter sales of $75.5 billion, up 26%; net income fell to $2.5 billion from $3.6 billion.
imageCaption: Amazon Prime delivery vans

headline: The best month since 1987, in the middle of a pandemic
text: With the Fed's emergency lending programmes and the 2 trillion dollar CARES Act behind them, shares more than won back their late-March losses, led by energy, consumer and health-care companies. The S&P 500 rose 13% in April to 2,912.43, its best month since January 1987, though still well below February's record and with unemployment soaring.
imageCaption: Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell at the Fed's video press conference, 29 April 2020

headline: Oil goes negative
text: OPEC, Russia and others agreed on 9 to 12 April to cut output by 9.7 million barrels a day, about 10% of world supply. It was not enough: on 20 April the expiring May contract for US crude fell to minus $37 a barrel, as storage at Cushing, Oklahoma filled up and holders paid to get rid of oil. Brent fell to about $9 the next day.
imageCaption: Crude oil storage at a US Strategic Petroleum Reserve site

headline: Schlumberger cuts its dividend by 75 percent
text: On 9 April Saudi Arabia and Russia agreed to cut output by about 10 million barrels a day; on 20 April US crude briefly fell to minus 37 dollars. On 17 April Schlumberger cut its quarterly dividend by 75 percent to 12.5 cents and took an 8.5 billion dollar charge, mostly writing down goodwill after the collapse in market values in March. Stock markets rebounded strongly from their lows.
imageCaption: An oil pumpjack in the Permian Basin, Texas

headline: Locked-down shoppers turn to eBay
text: On April 29 eBay reported first-quarter revenue of $2.4 billion, 174 million active buyers and gave a business update on Covid-19, which is sending shoppers online. Jamie Iannone has just become chief executive.
imageCaption: eBay's campus in Willow Glen, San Jose

headline: Profitable even in a pandemic quarter
text: On 29 April Tesla reported a profit for the first quarter, the first time it has been profitable in the seasonally weak first quarter, despite factory closures. It was its third profitable quarter in a row.
imageCaption: A Tesla Model 3, Xiamen, China

headline: ExxonMobil cuts spending by 30 percent as oil goes negative
text: On 7 April ExxonMobil cut its 2020 capital spending by 30 percent, from 33 to about 23 billion dollars, and cash operating costs by 15 percent, mostly in the Permian Basin. On 9 April Saudi Arabia and Russia agreed to cut output by about 10 million barrels a day. On 20 April the US crude price fell below zero, to minus 37 dollars, as storage ran out. Stocks rebounded strongly from their March lows.
imageCaption: The ExxonMobil Baytown complex seen across Goose Creek, Texas

headline: Sony to become Sony Group and buy out its finance arm
text: On 19 May Sony said it will rename itself Sony Group Corporation from April 2021, with the electronics business taking the Sony Corporation name, and will make Sony Financial Holdings, of which it owns about 65%, a wholly owned subsidiary through a takeover bid.
imageCaption: The Sony Building in the Ginza district, Tokyo

headline: Pandemic shoppers stock up at Walmart
text: Walmart reported that in the three months to April net sales rose 11% and online sales 74%, as Americans stocked up during the coronavirus lockdowns. Customers came less often but bought 16.5% more per visit, and profit rose 4% despite higher costs.
imageCaption: Pandemic shopping rules at a Walmart store, New York, 2020 ;;

headline: Stuck at home, the world goes online: Nasdaq above 10,000
text: The Nasdaq closed above 10,000 for the first time on 10 June, less than three months after falling to 6,861 on 23 March in the pandemic crash. With offices, shops and schools closed, people work, shop and learn online, and the largest technology companies have gained most.
imageCaption: The Nasdaq MarketSite tower in Times Square, New York

headline: Intel's 7-nanometre chips slip, and it may outsource
text: On 23 July Intel said its first 7-nanometre chips are six months later than planned, now due in late 2022 or early 2023, with production yields about a year behind target. Chief executive Bob Swan said Intel might have other companies make some chips. The shares fell 16% the next day.
source: https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/24/investing/intel-earnings-stock-selloff (read 2026-10-03, via search summary); https://siliconangle.com/2020/07/23/intels-stock-falls-delays-first-7nm-computer-chips/ (read 2026-10-03, via search summary)
imageCaption: Intel's D1X chip development factory under construction, Hillsboro, Oregon

headline: Two trillion dollars
text: On 19 August Apple's shares briefly topped 467 dollars, making it the first US company worth two trillion dollars, despite the pandemic. Apple has also announced that it will move its Macs from Intel processors to chips of its own design.
imageCaption: Apple Park, Cupertino

headline: Back at a record, five months after the crash
text: On 18 August the S&P 500 closed above its February record, less than five months after the March low. The S&P 500 rose 7% in August to 3,500.31, while the pandemic still kept much of the economy closed.
imageCaption: Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell at the Fed's press conference, 29 July 2020

headline: Gold at a record as the Fed says it will let inflation run
text: Gold averaged 1,969 dollars in August, beating its 2011 record. With the Fed's rate at zero, the 10-year Treasury yield averaged only 0.65 percent, below inflation of about 1 percent (July). On 27 August the Fed said it would now aim for inflation that 'averages 2 percent over time', allowing it to run 'moderately above 2 percent for some time' after periods below.
imageCaption: The gold vault of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York

headline: Tesla splits its shares five for one
text: On 11 August Tesla announced a five-for-one stock split, to make the shares more accessible to employees and investors; shareholders on record on 21 August receive four extra shares for each one. The shares rose 74% in August.
source: Tesla 8-K exhibit 'Tesla Announces a Five-for-One Stock Split', 11 August 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1318605/000156459020039353/tsla-ex991_6.htm (read 2026-10-03); data/out/tsla.json (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Nasdaq trading studio in Times Square, New York, where Tesla shares trade

headline: Siemens Energy is spun off
text: Shares of Siemens Energy, the former gas and power division, began trading in Frankfurt on 28 September after Siemens shareholders approved the split in July. Siemens shareholders received Siemens Energy shares; Siemens keeps a minority stake.
imageCaption: Siemens' gas turbine plant on Huttenstrasse, Berlin-Moabit

headline: Nvidia agrees to buy Arm for 40 billion dollars
text: On 13 September Nvidia agreed to buy Arm, the British designer of the processors in almost all smartphones, from SoftBank for 40 billion dollars, subject to approval by regulators; SoftBank would keep about 10% of Nvidia.
imageCaption: Arm's headquarters in Cambridge, England

headline: Regulators order Citigroup to fix 'longstanding deficiencies'
text: The Federal Reserve ordered Citigroup on 7 October to correct longstanding deficiencies in its risk management, data quality and internal controls, and its bank regulator fined it $400 million. In August Citibank had mistakenly wired $900 million to lenders of the cosmetics company Revlon. Jane Fraser, named in September, will succeed Michael Corbat as chief executive in February 2021, the first woman to lead one of the four biggest U.S. banks.
imageCaption: 388 Greenwich Street, Citigroup's headquarters in Lower Manhattan

headline: IBM to split off its old infrastructure services
text: On 8 October IBM announced it will spin off its managed infrastructure services unit into a separate listed company, keeping hybrid cloud and artificial intelligence. The unit runs IT for about 4,600 clients in 115 countries with a 60 billion dollar backlog. Chief executive Arvind Krishna, formerly head of IBM's cloud business and research, took over from Ginni Rometty in April and credits the Red Hat purchase with making the split possible.
imageCaption: Arvind Krishna, IBM's chief executive

headline: A vaccine, and the MAX is cleared to fly
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid-19 vaccine was more than 90% effective, and travel stocks soared. On 18 November the FAA ended the 737 MAX's 20-month grounding, the longest ever for a US airliner, subject to fixes on each plane and new pilot training.
imageCaption: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 MAX 8 at the gate

headline: Tesla will join the S&P 500
text: S&P Dow Jones Indices announced on 16 November that Tesla will join the S&P 500 index on 21 December, after five consecutive quarterly profits. Index funds will have to buy the shares; Tesla will be one of the ten most valuable companies in the index. The shares jumped more than 13% in after-hours trading.
source: CNBC, 'Tesla stock jumps on carmaker's addition to the S&P 500', 16 November 2020, https://www.cnbc.com/2020/11/16/tesla-stock-jumps-on-news-company-is-joining-sp-500.html (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The New York Stock Exchange, Wall Street

headline: Biden wins, and a vaccine works
text: Joe Biden won the US election of 3 November, with 306 electoral votes and about 51 percent of the vote, and was declared the winner by the media on 7 November; President Trump refuses to concede and claims fraud without evidence. On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech announced that their vaccine was about 90 percent effective in trials.
imageCaption: Crowds celebrate Joe Biden's election victory, Washington, 7 November 2020

headline: A vaccine lifts oil shares; ExxonMobil writes off up to 20 billion
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid vaccine was more than 90 percent effective in its first analysis, and oil shares, among the hardest hit by the pandemic, jumped. US crude rose from about 36 to 45 dollars during the month. On 30 November ExxonMobil said it would take a 17 to 20 billion dollar write-down on gas fields it no longer plans to develop, cut spending further and reduce its workforce by 15 percent by the end of 2021, while keeping the dividend.
source: Pfizer and BioNTech press release of 9 November 2020 (BioNTech Form 6-K exhibit 99.1), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1776985/000156459020052228/ (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 30 November 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000093/xomexhibit9911302020.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Darren Woods, chairman and chief executive of ExxonMobil

headline: Vaccine hopes send BMW up 28%
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech reported that their coronavirus vaccine is 90% effective, and stock markets surged, led by the shares that had suffered most in the lockdowns, such as car makers.
source: The Guardian, 'Global stock markets surge after Pfizer Covid vaccine news', 9 November 2020, https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/nov/09/stock-markets-covid-vaccine-ftse-100-coronavirus (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: A vial of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, December 2020

headline: Vaccine news sends bank shares soaring
text: Pfizer said on 9 November that its experimental COVID-19 vaccine, developed with BioNTech, was more than 90% effective in a large trial. Investors bought the shares hurt most by the pandemic, banks among them, and Citigroup's rose 33% in November.
imageCaption: Moderna's coronavirus vaccine being inspected, December 2020

headline: Disney+ passes 73 million subscribers in its first year
text: On 12 November Disney reported a loss for its business year because of the pandemic, but said Disney+ had more than 73 million paying subscribers after one year, 'far surpassing our expectations'.
imageCaption: Disney+

headline: A vaccine sends travel stocks soaring
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid-19 vaccine was more than 90% effective in trials. Shares of companies tied to travel jumped. General Electric had already promised at least 2.5 billion dollars of industrial free cash flow in the fourth quarter.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pfizer%E2%80%93BioNTech_COVID-19_vaccine (read 2026-10-03, citing NPR and STAT 2020-11-09); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/40545/000004054520000057/ge3q2020ex99.htm (GE third-quarter 2020 release, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: A GE90 engine at sunset on a Boeing 777

headline: Vaccine rally
text: Pfizer and BioNTech reported in November that their Covid-19 vaccine was highly effective in late-stage trials, and stock markets rose about 11%, led by the shares hit hardest in the pandemic. Copper averaged $7,069 a tonne, above its pre-Covid level, and coal rose to $64.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pfizer%E2%80%93BioNTech_COVID-19_vaccine; World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages; data/news/arcs/movers.md (all read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Pfizer-BioNTech Covid-19 vaccine, December 2020

headline: A vaccine and a decided election: shares up 11 percent
text: After the presidential election of 3 November, uncertainty fell, and on 9 November Pfizer's announcement of a successful vaccine trial set off a rush into the companies hurt most by the pandemic, such as travel and energy. The Dow closed above 30,000 for the first time on 24 November, and the S&P 500 rose 11% in November to 3,621.63.
imageCaption: Crowds celebrate in Farragut Square, Washington, after the election is called for Joe Biden, 7 November 2020

headline: 'Accelerating the Arches': digital, delivery and drive-thru
text: On 9 November chief executive Chris Kempczinski announced a new growth strategy, 'Accelerating the Arches', focused on marketing, core menu items (burgers, chicken and coffee) and the 'three Ds': digital, delivery and drive-thru, which proved their worth during the pandemic.
imageCaption: A McDonald's delivery bicycle ;;

headline: Vaccine news sends car shares soaring
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech reported that their coronavirus vaccine is 90% effective, and stock markets surged worldwide, led by shares that suffer most from lockdowns, such as car makers. Joe Biden's win in the US presidential election added to the optimism.
source: The Guardian, 'Global stock markets surge after Pfizer Covid vaccine news', 9 November 2020, https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/nov/09/stock-markets-covid-vaccine-ftse-100-coronavirus (read 2026-10-03); WSJ, 'Dow Surges to Highest Level Since February on Vaccine Results, Biden Win', 9 November 2020 (headline via Google News) (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: A vial of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, December 2020

headline: Vaccine news lifts the market
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech reported that their COVID-19 vaccine prevented about 91% of symptomatic infections in a trial with over 40,000 people. Stock markets jumped: the S&P 500 rose 11% in November.
imageCaption: Vials of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine

headline: Vaccine news lifts oil
text: Pfizer and BioNTech reported in November that their coronavirus vaccine met its efficacy goals in trials. Investors bet on a return to travel, and US crude rose 27% in the month to $45.20.
imageCaption: Vials of the Pfizer-BioNTech Covid-19 vaccine, 2020

headline: A vaccine sends oilfield shares soaring
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid vaccine was more than 90 percent effective in its first analysis. Shares hit hardest by the pandemic jumped; US crude rose from about 36 to 45 dollars during the month. Schlumberger rose almost 40 percent from its lowest month-end price since the mid-1990s.
source: Pfizer and BioNTech press release of 9 November 2020 (BioNTech Form 6-K exhibit 99.1), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1776985/000156459020052228/ (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); data/out/slb.json
imageCaption: A drillship seen across Brunei Bay

headline: Vaccine hopes lift the banks
text: Pfizer and BioNTech reported in November that their coronavirus vaccine had met its efficacy goals in the final trial, with a potential efficacy of more than 90%. Share markets rallied; the S&P 500 gained about 11% in the month. At UBS, Ralph Hamers took over as chief executive from Sergio Ermotti on 1 November.
imageCaption: Vials of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine

headline: Disney+ reaches 86.8 million; Disney raises its streaming targets
text: At an investor day on 10 December Disney said Disney+ had 86.8 million subscribers, a year after launch, and laid out plans for dozens of new Marvel and Star Wars series and films for streaming.
imageCaption: Disney+

headline: Glasenberg to retire; Nagle, the coal boss, to succeed
text: On 4 December Glencore said Ivan Glasenberg, chief executive since 2002, will step down in the first half of 2021, to be succeeded by Gary Nagle, 45, who runs its coal business from Sydney. The same day it set a target to cut its total emissions 40% by 2035 from 2019 levels and an ambition of net zero by 2050, by running down its coal mines rather than selling them. China has stopped buying Australian coal.
imageCaption: Ivan Glasenberg, Glencore's chief executive (left), March 2019
